Non-specific interstitial pneumonia (NSIP), cellular. The pure cellular form of NSIP is rare. If small poorly formed granulomas are present, hypersensitivity pneumonitis should be considered. If foci of organising pneumonia are present, without granulomas, cryptogenic organising pneumonia should be considered. H&E stain, 40xoriginal magnification.

Granulomatous pneumonia from infection. This example of atypical mycobacterial infection (Mycobacterium avium complex) differs from hypersensitivity pneumonitis in having larger and better formed granulomas, along with more granulomas in the alveolar spaces and alveolar ducts. Necrosis in granulomas may be present (not in this image) and is a harbinger of infection. Sarcoidosis granulomas (fig 25) are better formed, have less associate inflammation, and consistently have more hyaline fibrosis around aggregated granulomas. H&E stain, 40xoriginal magnification.

full.description: This image is a photomicrograph of lung tissue stained with hematoxylin and eosin (H&E). It shows alveolar spaces filled with an accumulation of eosinophilic material, likely representing exudate or cellular debris within the parenchyma. The alveolar walls display thickening and infiltration by inflammatory cells. The findings are characteristic of an acute or subacute pathological process affecting the pulmonary alveoli, such as an organizing pneumonia pattern.

blind.description: This image is a micrograph showing lung tissue with features of cellular non-specific interstitial pneumonia. The alveolar spaces contain an accumulation of macrophages with only slight fibrous thickening of the alveolar walls. The H&E stained section demonstrates characteristic interstitial inflammation without well-formed granulomas. The overall histological appearance supports a diagnosis of cellular non-specific interstitial pneumonia.

random.description: This image is a photomicrograph of lung tissue stained with hematoxylin and eosin. The alveolar spaces are filled with dense, amorphous eosinophilic material and hyaline membranes. There is also interstitial thickening and inflammation present within the tissue. These histopathological findings are characteristic of diffuse alveolar damage, commonly seen in acute respiratory distress syndrome.
